content:
In yet another rather ironic episode involving Windows 11, Microsoft is reportedly continuing to distribute an outdated Intel driver through Windows Update, despite its own antivirus software, Microsoft Defender, identifying an associated component as a legitimate security threat. Even removing the offending driver apparently doesn't stop Windows Update from offering it again.
![A slide titled 'Secure and reliable by design' from the DQI Pillar Architecture presents strategies to move driver stacks to user mode, standardize with a Microsoft-maintained driver, and harden kernel mode, highlighting a visual comparison between 'User Mode' and 'Kernel Mode.'](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Secure-driver-design.webp)
Windows Update Continues To Offer A Nearly Four-Year-Old Intel Driver Containing A Component With A Known Security Vulnerability Dating Back To 2020
As uncovered by German publication Deskmodder, Microsoft Defender recently flagged a file named OpenHardwareMonitorLib.sys on an 11th-generation Intel NUC system, classifying it as VulnerableDriver:WinNT/Winring0, with a severe threat rating.
![A security alert window shows 'VulnerableDriver:WinNT/Winring0' with a severe threat level, active status, dated 25.11.2026 16:18, and categorized as 'Trojaner,' detailing the file path leading to OpenHardwareMonitorLib.sys.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/WinRIng0.jpg)
The file was traced back to Intel's Performance Driver Extension (version 1.0.0.38), a component of the Intel NUC Software Studio Service dating back to December 8, 2022.
After disabling the associated service and removing the driver package from the Windows Driver Store, the publication queried the Windows Update Agent API, only to discover that Microsoft was still offering the exact same driver version for download.
Further examination revealed that the package contains WinRing0 components embedded within a digitally signed DLL. Interestingly, scanning the downloaded package with Microsoft Defender did not produce any security warnings, potentially because the flagged driver is only extracted at runtime. The publication did not reinstall the package to conclusively verify this behavior.
For those unfamiliar, WinRing0 provides low-level hardware access to applications, including utilities that monitor temperatures, voltages, and other hardware parameters. However, a security vulnerability documented under CVE-2020-14979 can allow attackers to elevate their privileges on an already-accessible system.
Microsoft itself explicitly acknowledges that the detection is legitimate, rather than a false positive. This does not, however, necessarily indicate that an affected PC has been compromised.
![The image shows a detailed CVE-2020-14979 report indicating a vulnerability in EVGA Precision X1, with a CVSS 3.x base score of '7.8 HIGH.'](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/CVE.jpg)
Intel Has Known About The Issue Since At Least August 2025, And Even Recommends Discontinuing Use Of The Software
Perhaps the most concerning aspect of this discovery is that the issue is hardly new. An Intel Community forum thread from August 2025 describes virtually the same behavior, with users reporting recurring Defender warnings after Windows Update reinstalled the problematic driver.
![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-mobile.png)
![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-desktop.png)
An Intel customer support representative subsequently acknowledged the WinRing0 detections, explaining that NUC Software Studio had reached the end of its security support lifecycle.
In fact, Intel had already published a security advisory in December 2024 concerning separate vulnerabilities affecting the software, recommending that users uninstall or discontinue its use.
![An Intel advisory titled 'Intel NUC Software Studio Service Advisory' lists the advisory category as Software, impact of vulnerability as 'Escalation of Privilege, Denial of Service, Information Disclosure,' severity rating as HIGH, with both original release and last revised dates as 12/10/2024.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Intel-CVE.jpg)
The discovery also comes at a particularly awkward time for Microsoft, which has been promoting its Driver Quality Initiative alongside ongoing efforts to remove obsolete drivers from Windows Update to improve security and reliability.
While Intel's discontinued software is undoubtedly part of the problem, one would expect Microsoft's own security and update infrastructures to be better coordinated. After all, users shouldn't have to fight Windows Update to keep a driver that Microsoft's own antivirus considers vulnerable off their systems.
